excerpt: Common but differentiated responsibilities and environmental burden sharing explain how international law distributes duties for ecological harm across states with unequal histories, capacities, vulnerabilities, and development needs. This article examines Rio Principle 7, UNFCCC Article 3, Kyoto differentiation, Paris Agreement Article 2(2), historical responsibility, respective capabilities, climate finance, adaptation, technology transfer, loss and damage, transparency, biodiversity, trade tensions, human rights, and climate justice. It shows how CBDR-RC operates as doctrine, bargaining language, distributive principle, and political fault line. The article also addresses mitigation ambition, fossil-fuel transition, development space, finance gaps, debt, green industrial policy, and burden shifting. By connecting doctrine, institutions, case studies, and lawyer-facing workflows, it shows how environmental law struggles to convert shared planetary responsibility into fair, credible, and enforceable cooperation across contemporary international legal systems.
